title: Feature Engineering
text:
1. Creating Time-Based Features
Tourism data is strongly seasonal. Time features help models learn recurring patterns. Examples include:

Month, Quarter, Year
Day of the week (useful for high-frequency data)
Season indicators (e.g., summer/winter tourism peaks)
Holiday periods, such as Christmas or national holidays

title: Feature Engineering
text:
2. Lag Features
These capture how the number of tourists in previous periods influences future values. Examples:

Tourists lagged by 1 month
Lag 3, lag 6, lag 12 (to capture annual seasonality)

title: Feature Engineering
text:
3. Rolling Window Statistics
Rolling features smooth fluctuations and describe recent trends. Examples:

3-month moving average
12-month rolling sum (useful for year-over-year analysis)
Rolling standard deviation (volatility of tourism flows)

title: Feature Engineering
text:
4. Pandemic / Shock Indicators
Tourism is highly sensitive to global shocks. Examples:

COVID-19 lockdown periods
Political instability indicators
Natural disaster events

title: Feature Engineering
text:
5. Interaction Features
Interactions help models understand combined effects, such as: “Summer season” × “Low exchange rate”.

title: Feature Engineering
section: Creating new features based on the original dataset
text:
Creating new features based on the original dataset
Download the dataset and create a dictionary of dataframes, one for each KKR (country). Then, define a function to add features such as rolling means, lags, and group statistics (mean, standard deviation, coefficient of variation) based on different grouping variables (WON, RO). Finally, apply this function to each dataframe in the dictionary.


Code
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def add_features_to_df(df, tourist_col="D8R1"):
    
    # kopiowanie opcjonalne (bezpieczne)
    df = df.copy()

    # --- data ---
    df["data"] = pd.to_datetime(
        df["OKRES"].astype(str).str[:4] + "-" +
        df["OKRES"].astype(str).str[4:6] + "-01"
    )

    # --- sort ---
    df = df.sort_values(["KKR", "data"])

    # =========================
    # ROLLING (NA GRUPIE KKR)
    # =========================
    df["mean_last_3"] = df.groupby("KKR")[tourist_col].transform(lambda x: x.rolling(3).mean())
    df["mean_last_6"] = df.groupby("KKR")[tourist_col].transform(lambda x: x.rolling(6).mean())
    df["mean_last_9"] = df.groupby("KKR")[tourist_col].transform(lambda x: x.rolling(9).mean())
    df["mean_last_12"] = df.groupby("KKR")[tourist_col].transform(lambda x: x.rolling(12).mean())


    # =========================
    # LAGI (NA GRUPIE KKR)
    # =========================
    for i in range(1, 13):
        df[f"lag_{i}"] = df.groupby("KKR")[tourist_col].shift(i)

    # =========================
    # STATYSTYKI GRUPOWE
    # =========================
    def add_group_stats(df, group_col, prefix):
        grouped = df.groupby(group_col)[tourist_col]

        mean = grouped.transform("mean")
        std = grouped.transform("std")

        df[f"{prefix}_mean"] = mean
        df[f"{prefix}_sd"] = std
        df[f"{prefix}_cv"] = np.where(mean == 0, np.nan, std / mean)

        return df

    df = add_group_stats(df, "WON", "WON")
    df = add_group_stats(df, "RO", "RO")

    return df


Dataset is too large to deal with it in a notebook, so we will save enriched dataframes to separate CSV files for each KKR (country) and use them in the next steps of the project.
Thats the reason why we choose only 5 countries with the highest number of tourists in the original dataset.
Dataset for each coutry will separate file with name “tourist_kkr_{KKR}.csv” in the “synthetic data” folder.

title: Post collection imputation - Foreign Tourist In Poland
text: Pilot study for imputation - accommodation establishments

title: Post collection imputation - Foreign Tourist In Poland
text:
Type of accomodation establisments
Tourist accommodation establishments regardless of the type, owner, and location, as well as establishments with other purposes (not related to tourism) that are temporarily used by tourists (e.g., student dormitories, sports and recreation centers).
Tourist accommodation establishments classified into the following activity groups according to NACE Rev. 2 classification:

55.1 – hotels and similar accommodation,
55.2 – holiday and other short-stay accommodation,
55.3 – camping grounds, recreational vehicle parks and trailer parks. The study covers 20 types of tourist accommodation establishments.

title: Post collection imputation - Foreign Tourist In Poland
text:
About survey
KT-1: Report on the occupancy of tourist accommodation establishments:

Mandatory monthly survey of accommodation establishments with 10 or more bed-places.
Census survey of 14,859 establishments.
The deadline for submitting reports is the 10th day after the reporting month. In practice, establishments report throughout the entire month.
Unit response rate is approximately 80% and varies due to seasonality.
Item non-response pertains mostly to foreign tourist data.

title: Post collection imputation - Foreign Tourist In Poland
text:
About Data
Range of collected data

Establishment name, type, address and category of establishment
Months of operation
Rooms and bed places
Occupancy (tourists and nights spent) during the surveyed month
Occupancy (tourists and nights spent) by foreign tourists with respect to country of residence
Categorical and count data

title: Explanatory Data Analysis
text:
Reading a data
The synthetic data were generated using the synthetizer package available in R. Therefore, the pyreadr library is used to import the data into Python. The tourism dataset is stored in an .rds file and can be loaded using the following code:


Code
import pyreadr
df = pyreadr.read_r('synthetic data/WP9_S2_Tourism_synt.rds').popitem()[1]

title: Explanatory Data Analysis
text:
Libraries used in the analysis

pandas – used for data manipulation and analysis, including loading, filtering, transforming, and summarizing the dataset.
geopandas – used for working with geographical and spatial data. It allows us to connect tourism data with geographical information, such as voivodeships or other administrative regions, and create maps.
matplotlib.pyplot – used to create visualizations, such as bar charts, line charts, histograms, and other plots.
itables – used to display interactive data tables in the notebook. The show function displays DataFrames as interactive tables, while init_notebook_mode initializes the interactive table functionality.
itables.options – used to configure the behavior of itables, for example by controlling warnings about undocumented options.
seaborn – used to create statistical visualizations. It provides more advanced and visually appealing charts, such as distribution plots, boxplots, heatmaps, and categorical plots, and works together with matplotlib.

Structure of tourism data

Dataset description
The dataset contains information about tourism establishments and tourist activity in Poland. Each row represents an establishment, identified by its REGON number. The dataset includes information about the type and location of the establishment, as well as data on domestic and foreign tourists.
The main variables include:

REGON – unique identifier of the establishment.
RO – type of tourism establishment.
WON – voivodeship (województwo ) where the establishment is located.
KKR – country of origin of tourists.
D8R1 – number of foreign tourists.

Due to the large size of the dataset, further analyses will be limited to the five countries with the highest number of foreign tourists. This will allow us to reduce the size of the dataset while focusing on the most significant tourist markets.

The descriptive statistics show that the number of foreign tourists varies considerably across the observations. Most observations have a relatively small number of tourists, with a median of 3 and 50% of observations falling between 2 and 9 tourists. However, the mean is considerably higher at 14.55, which indicates that some observations have much larger values. The maximum value of 8,605 further confirms the presence of extreme observations. Overall, the distribution of the number of foreign tourists is strongly right-skewed, with most establishments reporting relatively low numbers and a small number of establishments attracting substantially more foreign tourists.

plt.figure(figsize=(8,4))

plt.xlabel(' ')

The analyzed period covers January 1, 2018, to December 31, 2020. As shown in the chart, there is a noticeable increase in the number of foreign tourists during the summer months, with the highest values recorded in July and August in both 2018 and 2019. In March 2020, a sharp decline in tourist numbers can be observed due to the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic. The lockdown measures led to a near-total halt in foreign tourism. Although the numbers began to rise again in the summer months, they reached only about 25% of the values from the summer of 2019. Towards the end of the year, as COVID-19 infections surged, additional accommodation facilities were shut down, which contributed to a further significant drop in the number of foreign tourists.

The analysis shows clear differences in the number of foreign tourists across countries and years. Germany stands out as the most important source market, with the highest total number of tourists in 2018 and a substantial decrease in 2019 and 2020. Ukraine also represents an important tourist market, with relatively high numbers of observations and a comparatively stable total number of tourists between 2018 and 2019.
A noticeable decline can be observed in 2020 for all analysed countries. This is particularly visible for Germany, France, Italy, Spain, the United Kingdom and the United States. The decrease is also reflected in the lower mean and median values for most countries, indicating a substantial reduction in tourist activity.
The distributions are strongly right-skewed. For most countries, the median number of tourists per observation is between 2 and 6, while the mean is considerably higher. This indicates that most establishments recorded relatively small numbers of foreign tourists, while a smaller number of establishments received substantially more tourists

Most Popular Tourist Destinations in Poland
When it comes to the most frequently visited places, Warsaw in the Mazowieckie Voivodeship and Kraków in the Małopolskie Voivodeship stand out as the top destinations (highlighted in dark blue).Together, these two cities attracted over 3 million tourists annually in both 2018 and 2019.
In 2020, a significant decline in tourist numbers was observed in these two regions due to the pandemic.That year, the most visited places were seaside cities and Wrocław , likely due to its proximity to the German border.


Summary
The results indicate that foreign tourism in Poland was geographically concentrated and strongly affected by the changes observed in 2020. Germany was the dominant foreign market among the selected countries, while the regional analysis highlights Małopolskie and Mazowieckie as particularly important areas for foreign tourism.

title: Feature Selection
text:
Open the associated notebook:
No extensive data preprocessing was performed prior to model development. The dataset originates from an official statistical survey and is already provided in a structured and standardised format, which reduces the need for additional transformations.
Only basic preprocessing steps were applied, including verification of data types and conversion of variables representing dates into a proper datetime format. This step was necessary to enable the creation of additional time-dependent variables.
No standardisation or scaling was applied during initial data preparation; however, explanatory variables were standardized later within the modeling pipeline for regularized regression models.
More advanced preprocessing techniques, such as outlier removal, smoothing, or data transformation, were intentionally avoided in order to preserve the original characteristics of the dataset, including seasonality, regional variation, and effects of external events.
Since the objective of the project is to evaluate imputation methods under realistic conditions, maintaining the original data structure was considered more appropriate than applying extensive preprocessing.

    276: 'Germany',

Corelation matrix
The correlation matrix between the features and the target variable (D8R1) is calculated and visualized using a heatmap. The corr() function from the pandas library is used to calculate the correlation coefficients, while the seaborn library is used to create the heatmap visualization.


Code
import numpy as np
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


# Colums to exclude
exclude_cols = ['REGON', 'OKRES', 'WON', 'KKR', 'NRW', 'D8R1', 'data', 'country_en']



# Lista krajów
countries = df['country_en'].dropna().unique()

# Pusta ramka do zbierania korelacji
all_corrs = pd.DataFrame()

# Iteracja po krajach
for country in countries:
    country_df = df[df['country_en'] == country]
    
    # Wybierz kolumny numeryczne (bez wykluczonych)
    numeric_cols = country_df.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns
    numeric_cols = [col for col in numeric_cols if col not in exclude_cols]
    
    # Oblicz korelacje z D8R1
    corr_series = country_df[numeric_cols].corrwith(country_df['D8R1']).dropna()
    
    # Dodaj do zbiorczej ramki
    all_corrs[country] = corr_series

# Transponujemy, żeby na osi X były kraje, na osi Y zmienne
all_corrs = all_corrs.T

# Rysujemy heatmapę
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 8))
sns.heatmap(all_corrs.T, annot=True, cmap='viridis', cbar=True, linewidths=0.5)
plt.title('Correlation of number of tourists with created features by Country', fontsize=14)
plt.xlabel('Country')
plt.ylabel('Variable')
plt.tight_layout()

plt.show()









The variables most strongly correlated with the dependent variable are the 2-, 6-, 9-, and 12-period moving averages. For some countries, a correlation is also observed between the average values at the municipality level and the corresponding standard deviation within the same municipality

title: Feature Selection
section: Regularized Linear Regression for Feature Selection
text:
Regularized Linear Regression for Feature Selection
Feature selection was performed using regularized linear regression models to identify the most relevant predictors of tourist numbers while reducing multicollinearity among explanatory variables.
Due to strong correlations between temporal variables (particularly lagged values and moving averages), regularization techniques were applied. Ridge regression was used for coefficient shrinkage and model stabilization, without performing feature selection. The regularization strength was selected using cross-validation.
To identify the most important predictors, Elastic Net regularization was additionally applied. By combining L1 and L2 penalties, this approach enables both coefficient shrinkage and automatic variable selection by shrinking less relevant coefficients to zero.
The analysis was conducted separately for each country using chronologically ordered training and testing datasets. Model performance was evaluated using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE).
Final variable selection was based on non-zero coefficient values, which identified the most informative predictors of tourist flows. Across all countries, autoregressive variables (lags) and moving averages were consistently the most important predictors, indicating strong temporal dependence in tourist arrivals.

from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeCV, LassoCV, ElasticNetCV
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

# lista zmiennych
features = [
    'mean_last_3', 'mean_last_6', 'mean_last_9', 'mean_last_12',
    'lag_1', 'lag_2', 'lag_3', 'lag_4', 'lag_5', 'lag_6',
    'lag_7', 'lag_8', 'lag_9', 'lag_10', 'lag_11', 'lag_12',
    'WON_mean', 'WON_sd', 'WON_cv',
    'RO_mean', 'RO_sd', 'RO_cv'
]

target = 'D8R1'

results = {}

# pętla po krajach
for country, data in df.groupby('country_en'):
    
    data = data.sort_values('data')  # ważne przy szeregach czasowych
    
    # drop NA (lagi itd.)
    data = data.dropna(subset=features + [target])
    
    if len(data) < 30:
        continue  # za mało danych
    
    X = data[features]
    y = data[target]
    
    # split czasowy (np. 80/20)
    split = int(len(data) * 0.8)
    X_train, X_test = X.iloc[:split], X.iloc[split:]
    y_train, y_test = y.iloc[:split], y.iloc[split:]
    
    # pipeline: skalowanie + model
    
    model = Pipeline([
        ('scaler', StandardScaler()),
        ('reg', RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-3, 3, 50)))
        # alternatywy:
        # ('reg', LassoCV(cv=5))
        # ('reg', ElasticNetCV(l1_ratio=[0.1, 0.5, 0.9]))
    ])
    
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    
    preds = model.predict(X_test)
    
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, preds))
    
    results[country] = {
        'model': model,
        'rmse': rmse
    }

# wyniki
results_df = pd.DataFrame({
    country: {'RMSE': res['rmse']}
    for country, res in results.items()
}).T

import os
#selekacja zmiennych przez Elastic Net
from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNetCV #regression model with regularization + automatic tuning
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler #standardizes features
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline #ensures scaling + model happen in correct order

selected_features_per_country = {} #Creating a container for results


#Loop over countries
#You split your dataset into separate subsets per country
# Each country gets its own model and feature selection


for country, data in df.groupby('country_en'):
    #Sorting by time
    data = data.sort_values('data')
    data = data.dropna(subset=features + [target]) #Removing missing values
    #Removes rows where: any feature is missing or target (D8R1) is missing

    if len(data) < 50: #Skip countries with too little data
        continue
    #X → input variables (lags, rolling means, stats)
    #y → what you want to predict (D8R1)
    X = data[features]
    y = data[target]
    
    model = Pipeline([
        ('scaler', StandardScaler()), #transforms each feature to:mean = 0, std = 1
        ('reg', ElasticNetCV(

            #ElasticNet combines:

#L1 (Lasso) → pushes some coefficients to exactly 0
#L2 (Ridge) → shrinks coefficients smoothly

#Controlled by:
            l1_ratio=[0.1, 0.5, 0.9],
            #0.1 → mostly Ridge
            #0.9 → mostly Lasso
            cv=5, #5-fold cross-validation to find best alpha and l1_ratio
            max_iter=10000
        ))
    ])
    
    model.fit(X, y)
    
    coefs = model.named_steps['reg'].coef_
    
    selected = [f for f, c in zip(features, coefs) if abs(c) > 1e-6]
    
    selected_features_per_country[country] = selected

# podejrzyj
for k, v in selected_features_per_country.items():
    print(k, ":", v)
